name: Least Prefix Sum
description: Baltic, a famous chess player who is also a mathematician, has an array $$$a_1,a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$, and he can perform the following operation several (possibly $$$0$$$) times: Choose some index $$$i$$$ ($$$1 \leq i \leq n$$$); multiply $$$a_i$$$ with $$$-1$$$, that is, set $$$a_i := -a_i$$$. Baltic's favorite number is $$$m$$$, and he wants $$$a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_m$$$ to be the smallest of all non-empty prefix sums. More formally, for each $$$k = 1,2,\ldots, n$$$ it should hold that $$$$$$a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_k \geq a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_m.$$$$$$ Please note that multiple smallest prefix sums may exist and that it is only required that $$$a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_m$$$ is one of them. Help Baltic find the minimum number of operations required to make $$$a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_m$$$ the least of all prefix sums. It can be shown that a valid sequence of operations always exists.
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \leq t \leq 10\,000$$$). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$m$$$ ($$$1 \leq m \leq n \leq 2\cdot 10^5$$$) — the size of Baltic's array and his favorite number. The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1,a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$-10^9 \leq a_i \leq 10^9$$$) — the array. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$2\cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, print a single integer — the minimum number of required operations.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1779C — Least Prefix Sum [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
